newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FEATURE-Australians look for bashed potato recipe.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Australians look for bashed potato recipe.

text.p: Australian molecular biologist Simon Robinson has done the easy work, genetically engineering a potato that does not turn brown when cut or bruised.
Now, with a tonne of them harvested, comes the hard bit -- how to prove scientifically that his perfect spuds have what it takes to stay white.
"We have tried hitting them with a swinging pendulum, shaking them in jars, dropping them from a height, dropping things on them and so on," Robinson says.

Robinson and his team, researchers with Australia's Commonwealth Scientific Industrial and Research Organisation (CSIRO) say they have developed the world's first non-browning potato by isolating and copying the gene, or DNA sequence, which makes potatoes turn brown and then inserting the copy back to front into the potato plant.
The team has just harvested a tonne of the potatoes grown under ideal commercial conditions.

But now it has to work out a scientifically acceptable method for bruising, replicating in the laboratory the damage done to many Australian potatoes that bump along for thousands of kilometres in the back of a truck.

"Believe it or not, people all around the world are worrying about this problem: some people have shaking tables, some hit them with marbles, but no-one can agree on what the most representative way is," says Robinson.
GOOD NEWS FOR FRENCH FRIES

It may not sound like high science in action, but the CSIRO believes the technology could yield it millions of dollars -- not through domestic shoppers and cooks who get turned off by bruised or browned potatoes or other fruit and vegetables, but through food processors who stand to save big money.

Robinson said the CSIRO is working on commercial varieties of potatoes that end up as potato crisps or French fries, where discolouration costs an estimated A$10 million a year for rejected potatoes in Australia alone.

The technology is also expected to be put to work at some time for apples, pears, bananas and lettuces. But again it would be used in the processed commercial end of the market -- for pre-packed salads in supermarkets or fast food outlets -- rather than at the greengrocers.
"If we could see a benefit to the consumer in doing something in the fresh market, we would, and in the case of bananas, we will," Robinson says.
"But if you have a position that is worth something, obviously you have to license it to someone who is going to make money out of it."
Another factor in not immediately approaching the fresh food market is doubts over the acceptance by consumers of genetically engineered food, Robinson says.
These doubts are shared by Australia's leading French fry processors, who are not rushing -- publicly at least -- to the CSIRO's field.
Milton Rodda, field manager with McCains, a subsidiary of Canada's McCain group, said bruising could affect up to 30 percent of potatoes.
Although it was certainly interested in the CSIRO's research, McCains had to be convinced that consumers were ready to accept genetically altered foods, he said.
"It is easy to rush out and get excited about these types of things, but I think we have to tread carefully with it," he said.
LOOK, BUT DON'T TASTE
Scientists in the United States are already far advanced with other types of genetically-altered potatoes, for example potatoes resistant to beetles.
The CSIRO expects its process to affect only one characteristic of potatoes -- the browning gene.
So far, its trial is running to plan: the potatoes look normal, fit commercial size requirements, and have the right colour when fried.

The team expects them also to taste the same but, curiously, they are not allowed to try them yet until they have been tested -- as any new natural breeds must be -- for a toxin occasionally found in wild and green potatoes.
"At this stage there is no reason for us to want to eat them. There is no reason to believe they will taste any different to other potatoes," Robinson said.
Despite similar research on browning in the United States and Holland, the CSIRO believes it has a strong patent position for the process.

It has already signed a licensing agreement with the Canadian group Okanagan Biotechnology Inc to employ the as yet undeveloped process in apples and pears and another, yet to be announced, for lettuces and bananas.
In the meantime, what about establishing the perfect bruising technique?
"I think it is one of those things scientists will sit down in the evenings and talk about for the rest of their lives," Robinson laughs.
